content: Cobalt is a chemical element represented by the symbol Co and has an atomic number of 27. It naturally occurs only in chemically combined forms and not as a free element. When isolated through reductive smelting, cobalt appears as a hard, lustrous, silver-gray metal. Historically, cobalt-based blue pigments, known as cobalt blue, have been used since ancient times for jewelry, paints, and imparting a distinctive blue tint to glass. Early alchemists mistakenly attributed this blue color to the metal bismuth. Miners referred to certain cobalt-containing minerals as kobold ore (German for goblin ore) because these ores were poor in known metals and emitted toxic arsenic-containing fumes during smelting. In 1735, these ores were found to yield a new metal, cobalt, marking the first discovery of a new metal since ancient times. Today, cobalt is primarily obtained as a by-product of copper and nickel mining, with the largest global production coming from the Copper Belt in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. Cobalt is mainly used in the production of magnetic, wear-resistant, and high-strength alloys. Its compounds, such as cobalt silicate and cobalt(II) aluminate, are used to produce a deep blue color in glass, ceramics, inks, paints, and varnishes. Cobalt naturally exists as a single stable isotope, cobalt-59, while cobalt-60 is a commercially significant radioisotope used as a radioactive tracer and for generating high-intensity gamma rays. Cobalt is an essential trace dietary mineral for all animals, as it forms the active center of coenzymes called cobalamins, the most common of which is vitamin B12. Inorganic cobalt is also a vital nutrient for bacteria, algae, and fungi. While pure cobalt does not occur naturally, cobalt compounds are widespread in rocks, soil, plants, and animals. Cobalt is often associated with nickel in nature and is a minor component of meteoric iron. It has two crystallographic structures, hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and face-centered cubic (fcc), with a transition temperature of approximately 450°C. Cobalt is resistant to oxidation due to a passivating oxide film but reacts with halogens and sulfur. When heated in oxygen, it forms cobalt(II,III) oxide (Co3O4), which decomposes to cobalt(II) oxide (CoO) at higher temperatures. Cobalt exhibits common oxidation states of +2 and +3, with compounds ranging from -3 to +4. Cobalt(II) salts form red-pink complexes in aqueous solutions, while the addition of chloride produces intensely blue complexes. Cobalt oxides, such as CoO, Co3O4, and Co2O3, are known, with CoO being antiferromagnetic at low temperatures. Cobalt also forms sulfides, such as CoS2 and Co2S3, and halides, including cobalt(II) fluoride, chloride, bromide, and iodide, which exist in both anhydrous and hydrated forms. Cobalt forms coordination complexes with various ligands, and its chemistry is influenced by principles of electronegativity and ligand hardness. For example, cobalt(III) complexes often feature ammine ligands, while softer ligands like phosphines stabilize cobalt(I) and cobalt(II) states. Cobalt is also a key component in organometallic compounds, such as cobaltocene and cobalt carbonyl, which serve as catalysts in industrial reactions. Cobalt-59 is the only stable isotope of cobalt, while cobalt-60 is a radioactive isotope used in medical and industrial applications, including radiotherapy and gamma-ray production. Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years and is used in devices like Mössbauer spectroscopy and X-ray fluorescence. Improper disposal of cobalt-60 sources has led to serious radiation contamination incidents. Cobalt has been used for centuries to impart a rich blue color to glass, ceramics, and glazes. It was detected in ancient Egyptian sculptures, Persian jewelry, and Chinese artifacts. The term cobalt originates from the German word kobold, meaning goblin, reflecting miners' superstitions about the toxic fumes released during smelting. Swedish chemist Georg Brandt is credited with discovering cobalt around 1735, distinguishing it as a new element responsible for the blue color in glass. Cobalt is primarily produced as a by-product of nickel and copper mining. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is the leading producer, with significant reserves in the Katanga Province. Various methods, including froth flotation and roasting, are used to separate cobalt from other metals. The resulting cobalt oxide is reduced to metallic cobalt through aluminothermic reactions or carbon reduction in blast furnaces. Cobalt is widely used in high-performance alloys, particularly cobalt-based superalloys, which are valued for their temperature stability and resistance to corrosion and wear. These alloys are used in turbine blades, jet engines, and orthopedic implants. Cobalt alloys, such as stellite and vitallium, are also used in dental prosthetics and high-speed steel tools. Cobalt is a key component in permanent magnets, such as Alnico and samarium-cobalt magnets, and is alloyed with platinum for jewelry. Cobalt compounds are used in lithium-ion battery cathodes, where lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2) facilitates energy storage and release. Cobalt is also present in nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries, enhancing nickel's oxidation capabilities. In catalysis, cobalt compounds are used in oxidation reactions, such as converting xylene to terephthalic acid, and in the Fischer-Tropsch process for synthesizing liquid fuels. Cobalt is essential for life in trace amounts, as it is a key component of vitamin B12. Ruminant animals rely on gut bacteria to convert cobalt salts into vitamin B12, while non-ruminants must obtain the vitamin from their diet. Cobalt deficiencies in soil have historically caused livestock health issues, which were resolved by supplementing fertilizers with cobalt salts. While cobalt is vital in small amounts, excessive exposure can be toxic. Chronic cobalt ingestion has caused health problems, and cobalt compounds added to beer in the 1960s led to a condition known as beer drinker's cardiomyopathy. Cobalt is also a common cause of contact dermatitis. Proper handling and disposal of cobalt, particularly radioactive isotopes, are essential to prevent health and environmental hazards.
